title: Lake or tube: which presses harder?
hook: A huge lake and a thin tube, both 10 m of water. Surely the lake squeezes harder?

knows: deeper water squeezes harder (ears hurt at the bottom of a pool)
doesNotKnow: P = rho g h for a still liquid
that the width or shape of the container does not change the pressure at a given depth

misconception: A wide lake pushes harder at the bottom than a thin tube of water of the same depth.
objective: The learner can explain that water pressure depends only on depth (rho g h), so a 10 m lake and a 10 m tube both give 98.1 kPa at the bottom; the lake's bottom just has more area.

claims.text: In still fresh water, the pressure 10 m down (not counting the air above) is about 98.1 kPa, whatever the width of the container.
claims.source: Hydrostatics, P = rho g h = 1000 x 9.81 x 10 = 98,100 Pa. Re-derived by integrating dP/dz = rho g down a column in artifacts/scratch/w4phys/check.mjs: 98.10 kPa at 10 m; 19.62 to 196.20 kPa for the stage's 2-20 m depths. No width term appears.

claims.text: Pressure at a depth is the weight of the column of water straight above each square metre, so a wider lake adds columns side by side, not taller ones.
claims.source: OpenStax University Physics Vol. 1, section 14.1 Fluids, Density, and Pressure, subsection Variation of Pressure with Depth (the column argument); the hydrostatic paradox (Stevin, 1586; Pascal).

claims.text: The lake's whole bottom carries far more total force than the tube's, spread over far more area.
claims.source: Total force on a flat bottom = P x A; at equal P, a larger area carries proportionally more force.

claims.text: Model: still fresh water at 1000 kg/m³ and g = 9.81 m/s²; the reading is gauge pressure (air pressure on the surface not counted). The stage's widths are not drawn to scale; its depths are.
claims.source: Stated on stage ('Depth to scale; widths not to scale. Fresh water.') and in the reveal. Including the atmosphere would add about 101 kPa to every reading equally.

recall.question: A narrow well and a wide reservoir are both filled to 6 m deep with water. Which has the greater water pressure at the bottom?
recall.why: Water pressure depends only on depth (rho g h), about 59 kPa at 6 m in both. The reservoir's bottom just has more area, so more total force.
